articles.excerpt: James Devonport built a small device: an e-ink display on his desk that periodically shows train departures. I like it. It is not a huge project, but it is useful. A quick glance gives you the informa…
articles.body: James Devonport built a small device: an e-ink display on his desk that periodically shows train departures. I like it. It is not a huge project, but it is useful. A quick glance gives you the information without unlocking a phone or opening another web page. If I made one, I would probably start with my blog: whether the site is reachable, when I last published, and whether anything needs attention. Two or three things are enough. More would be too much to scan. After reading his article , though, my first thought was not to buy the hardware. It was how to build this without creating a maintenance chore. Keep cloud work out of the device James uses an ESP32-based Note4C, Cloudflare Workers and help from Codex.

articles.title: The More I Develop with AI, the Less I Skip the Process
articles.excerpt: I use AI to work on my blog now: features, styling, translation and deployment all involve it. It is genuinely convenient. But the more I do this, the clearer one thing becomes: AI can write the code;…
articles.body: I use AI to work on my blog now: features, styling, translation and deployment all involve it. It is genuinely convenient. But the more I do this, the clearer one thing becomes: AI can write the code; that does not make the development process optional. On Weiyi, cramped typography means changing the type. A table cut off on a phone means fixing the table. Those changes are straightforward, and opening the page afterward tells me a lot. Multilingual content, analytics and backend APIs are different. A normal-looking page does not prove correct behavior. A successful build does not prove production is fine. Where I am unsure, I do not let AI invent the answer A six-language blog sounds like translating Chinese into five other languages. There is much more to it.

articles.title: CF7 Form Data Validation Before Sending to API: A Complete Implementation Guide
articles.excerpt: You have a Contact Form 7 form connected to an external API. The form submits. The plugin fires the API request. And then the API rejects it—because the email domain is blocked, the phone number forma…
articles.body: You have a Contact Form 7 form connected to an external API. The form submits. The plugin fires the API request. And then the API rejects it—because the email domain is blocked, the phone number format is wrong for that specific service, or the field value violates a business rule the API enforces. The user sees a generic success message. The API log shows a failure. And you have no way to tell the user what went wrong before the request was even sent. This is the validation gap. CF7 validates what it knows: required fields, email format, file size. It does not know your API's rules. Bridging that gap requires custom validation that runs before the API request fires. Why CF7's Built-in Validation Is Not Enough Contact Form 7 provides default validation for common field types.

articles.title: Scope Creep Starts Young: Teaching Students to Ship One Small Coding Project a Week
articles.excerpt: Every developer has a graveyard of side projects. Big idea, great first weekend, then scope creep, then silence. Students learning to code hit exactly the same wall, just earlier. The fix we use with…
articles.body: Every developer has a graveyard of side projects. Big idea, great first weekend, then scope creep, then silence. Students learning to code hit exactly the same wall, just earlier. The fix we use with students in Classes 6–12 is borrowed straight from how working teams ship: small scope, fixed requirements, short iterations . We call it Mini-Project Monday . The spec: one sentence, three requirements Before writing code, the student writes a tiny spec: goal: "Roll two dice and announce the winner." must_have: - roll two random numbers (1-6) - display both rolls - announce the higher roll as the winner later: - best of 5 rounds - player names - dice images Rules: The goal must fit in one sentence . If it doesn't, cut scope. Exactly three must-haves. Not "about three".

articles.title: Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
articles.excerpt: Satellites are watching fireballs blaze through Earth's atmosphere, strengthening planetary defense knowhow and helping scientists learn more about space debris impacts.
articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.excerpt: It's unclear at the moment exactly when and where the Swift observatory will plunge to Earth. But researchers definitely have their eyes peeled.
articles.body: NASA's Swift space telescope is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will reenter Earth's atmosphere in an uncontrolled fashion, after a robotic rescue mission failed to boost the scope to a higher orbit. Swift launched to Earth orbit back in November 2004. Over the next two decades, it studied gamma-ray bursts — the most powerful explosions in the universe — and other cosmic objects and events using a trio of telescopes: a Burst Alert Telescope (BAT), an X-Ray Telescope (XRT), and its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT). articles.title: 5 bright planets to spot in November — when and where to see them
articles.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn , visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight. Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
